info.bio:
Bachman-Turner Overdrive fue un grupo canadiense de hard rock, fundado en 1972.

Formado por Randy Bachman, cantante y guitarrista que venía de la banda The Guess Who. Tras dejar esta banda, Randy grabó un disco en solitario (Axe, 1970) y posteriormente intentó formar otra banda junto con el líder de The Nice, el teclista Keith Emerson, el cual pasaría más tarde a formar parte del trío Emerson, Lake & Palmer, aunque el proyecto quedó aparcado por culpa de una enfermedad de Bachman.

scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El hard rock marca el fin de los creativos sesenta: sigue basado en el blues, pero más rápido, ruidoso y fuerte, y entierra el sufrimiento negro bajo miles de decibelios. Precedido por Cream, Blue Cheer y Guess Who, lo definen Led Zeppelin, hijos del blues que lo tocan como música para el cuerpo y que imponen el LP como formato del rock. En Gran Bretaña, Free, Status Quo, Thin Lizzy, UFO, Uriah Heep, Slade, Faces, Deep Purple (el estereotipo del género), Black Sabbath (cimientos del black y el doom metal) y Queen, los bromistas del movimiento. En EE UU, Mountain, James Gang, Grand Funk Railroad, Montrose, Bachman-Turner Overdrive y Heart.

podcast.title: Formation (1970)
podcast.body: Following Randy Bachman's departure from The Guess Who in 1970, he co-founded a new band, Bachman-Turner Overdrive, with former Guess Who member Chad Allan, his brother Robbie Bachman, and bassist Fred Turner. "He left the guest who in 1970 and with another former band member Chad Allen and Backman's brother Robbie and bassist red turner, they formed a new band."

podcast.title: "Car Music" Description
podcast.body: Randy Bachman described Bachman-Turner Overdrive's music as "car music," meaning the kind of music specifically designed for listening to while driving. "Backman said that they make car music, the type you want to listen to while you're driving."

podcast.title: Band Name Origin
podcast.body: The band's name, Bachman-Turner Overdrive (BTO), originated from a trucking magazine called "Overdrive" that they encountered at a steakhouse in Windsor, Ontario. "the name came from a trucking magazine that they saw at a steakhouse in Windsor, Ontario. The name of the magazine was Overdrive."

podcast.title: Early Success and Domestic Acceptance
podcast.body: Bachman-Turner Overdrive (BTO) had success as far back as the 1960s, but like many Canadian groups, domestic acceptance and popularity only came after they had a hit in America. This pattern highlights the historical bias where external validation was crucial for Canadian artists at home. "The guests who BTO Rush, Triumph, April Wine and others had success as far back as the 1960s. But in most cases, domestic acceptance and popularity only came after these groups had a hit in America."

podcast.title: Fred Turner's Role in Naming
podcast.body: Fred Turner proposed the band name by writing "BTO" on a napkin, which the members found appealing because "Overdrive" aptly described their musical style. "Fred Turner, he took a napkin, he wrote BTO on it. He's like, what do you think about this? They liked it because Overdrive seemed like a good descriptor of their style of music."

podcast.title: Increased FM Airplay
podcast.body: Due to new FM radio rules in Canada that mandated playing more album tracks and Canadian content, Bachman-Turner Overdrive's music, alongside others like The Guess Who and Neil Young, saw significantly more airplay. This was in part because there weren't enough new Canadian bands of a certain caliber yet. "a lot more guest who, back then turn or overdrive the band and Neil Young got played."

podcast.title: Mid-1980s Domestic & International Success
podcast.body: By the mid-1980s, BTO was among several Canadian rock acts that released albums performing "extremely well domestically and internationally," some even achieving multi-platinum sales in foreign markets. "Rush, April Wine, BTO, Loverboy, Triumph, Brian Adams, and a half a dozen others all released albums that had done extremely well domestically and internationally."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Strict Band Conduct and Tim Bachman's Firing
podcast.body: Randy Bachman enforced strict behavioral rules for his new bandmates, including prohibitions on drinking, drugs, and pre-marital sex. This commitment to "straight-laced behavior" was so strong that his brother, Tim Bachman, was fired from the band, with strong belief that it was for not adhering to these regulations. "He was serious, though, about the type of straight lace behavior that he expected from his new bandmates so much so that he fired his brother Tim and it's strongly believed that Tim was fired for not adhering to these rules."

xref.title: Hip-Hop Influence on Guitar Style
xref.body: Despite playing in bands that covered rock acts like Led Zeppelin, Bachman-Turner Overdrive, and Black Sabbath, Tom Morello was profoundly influenced by Run DMC and Public Enemy. This led him to develop a unique guitar style that involved scratching the strings, mimicking a DJ's turntable technique. "Although these bands covered songs like Led Zeppelin, Bachminton, Overdrive, and Black Sabbath, Tom was profoundly affected by run DMC in public enemy. That's how his guitar style developed, scratching the strings, like a DJ would scratch on a turntable."
